transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-05-26
Time: 11:00 AM PDT
Duration: ~39 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Sofia Martinez (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (AtlasPay Head of ML), Mark Davis (AtlasPay Infra), Olivia Chen (AtlasPay PM)
---
[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll give it a quick agenda — model selection updates, the pinning strategy for the pilot, and fallback/rollback runbook. Sofia and I are here from Redwood. 
[00:23] Priya Rao: Hi all, Priya here. We've got Mark and Olivia on our side. Quick note — been running the staging harness overnight, saw a couple of strange tokenization differences in the billing prompts. Not a blocker but wanted to flag.
[00:45] Sofia Martinez: Got it, Priya. We'll look at tokenizer differences; sometimes quantized kernels change whitespace behavior slightly. Can you paste an example in the Slack thread after?
[00:58] Mark Davis: Yep I'll drop it in. Also, throughput numbers from our internal benchmark — p95 is around 420ms on your hosted endpoint when we use model-x-3b-v1-quant.
[01:15] Alex Chen: Thanks Mark. Quick callout on naming — Redwood's catalog currently has model-x-3b-v1-quant and the non-quantized model-x-3b-v1. For the pilot we usually recommend pinning to a specific model version and then using a fallback policy to a compatible variant.
[01:40] Olivia Chen: Can you explain the difference between pinning and routing fallback? We want predictable behavior for compliance reviews.
[01:50] Sofia Martinez: Sure. Pinning means the pilot will always hit the exact model artifact you approve — e.g., model-x-3b-v1-quant. Routing fallback is a policy that says if that model's capacity is exhausted or latency breaches, route to a defined compatible model, like model-x-3b-v1 (non-quant) or model-x-6b-v1 on a higher tier. Pinning avoids surprise model changes when we do catalog updates.
[02:20] Priya Rao: That's good. Our security team requires a clear list of approved binaries. So pinning makes audits easier. If we fallback we need audit logs. Does Redwood capture that?
[02:35] Alex Chen: Yes — audit logs show the exact model id, timestamp, and route decision. We'll include a sample log output.
[02:45] Mark Davis: One operational question — if we pin to a quantized variant, and we see a quality regression on a handful of prompts, what's the recommended rollback path?
[03:00] Sofia Martinez: Two patterns we've used: 1) Canary with traffic split — send 5-10% of traffic to the pinned quantized model and compare eval metrics; if metrics degrade beyond your threshold, automated rollback to the non-quantized version. 2) Instant fallback: if the endpoint's health or latency SLO breaks, route to the fallback model immediately. Both can be combined with a monitoring threshold.
[03:30] Priya Rao: For our use case, we care about hallucination and exact-matching for billing line items, so we need a strict quality gate. Can Redwood surface those metrics in the console?
[03:45] Alex Chen: Yes — Redwood Console supports custom evals and alerting. You can upload a prompt set and define pass/fail thresholds; Console will track regression and send alerts. For the POC we can wire your prompt set into the eval harness.
[04:05] Olivia Chen: What's the typical delta in latency/cost between quantized and non-quantized in your experience? Mark's number seemed low already.
[04:18] Sofia Martinez: Rough ballpark — quantized can cut token-cost by 30-60% and improve throughput depending on hardware. Latency often improves slightly per-token but sometimes increases for the first token due to kernel paths. The difference depends on sequence length and KV cache hit rates.
[04:40] Mark Davis: Our traffic is short prompts, p50 ~ 80 tokens. So benefits should be visible. But concerned about first-byte latency since our UI SLO is p95 < 300ms.
[04:55] Alex Chen: Right — for short prompts you see more benefit at higher batch sizes. For p95 under 300ms, we should test both pinned variants at expected concurrency. Sofia will run a 1k-sample run matching your traffic shape.
[05:10] Sofia Martinez: I'll do that. Question for AtlasPay: do you want us to test FP16 vs 4-bit quant? 4-bit yields more cost savings but increases risk of subtle output shifts.
[05:25] Priya Rao: Let's start with FP16 and one 4-bit candidate. We'll validate quality on our key prompt set. If 4-bit is OK, we can consider it for lower-priority flows.
[05:38] Olivia Chen: Sounds reasonable. On fallback capacity — if the pinned model is out of capacity, how do we ensure routing doesn't route to a higher-cost model unintentionally? We need cost guardrails.
[05:52] Alex Chen: You can define routing policy that prefers cheaper compatible variants and sets a cap on cost per request. The policy can also trigger a throttled queue instead of routing to a more expensive model. We'll share a sample policy template.
[06:10] Mark Davis: Can we set a daily spend cap for the pilot environment?
[06:16] Alex Chen: Yes — Redwood quotas let you set per-project spend limits and hard caps. If the cap is reached, traffic is rejected or falls back to on-prem/local model if configured.
[06:30] Priya Rao: Okay, shifting to pinning logistics — once we pin, how do we handle model updates? E.g., security patch or new version — does pinning block automatic updates?
[06:45] Sofia Martinez: Pinning blocks automatic catalog upgrades. You can create a release and schedule a controlled rollout. When a new model version is available, Redwood treats it as a separate model id; you decide when to switch.
[06:58] Olivia Chen: Good. For audit, we need a changelog of model switches.
[07:04] Alex Chen: That's in audit logs — model id and who made the change. We'll include an example.
[07:15] [07:15] Mark Davis: Quick nit — in the staging runs I noticed tokenization mismatch for a currency string, like "$1,200" becomes "$1 200" in one output. Might be whitespace normalization from the tokenizer.
[07:30] Sofia Martinez: Please paste that example. It might be a locale tokenization edge-case. We can try different tokenizers or post-processing rules.
[07:45] Priya Rao: We'll add those examples to the prompt set.
[08:00] Alex Chen: Moving on — can we agree on the pin candidate? Based on your perf numbers and quality, recommendation is model-x-3b-v1-quant (FP16 candidate) as primary pin, with fallback to model-x-3b-v1 (non-quant). And keep model-x-6b-v1 as an emergency fallback only.
[08:25] Priya Rao: I like FP16 as a compromise. We'll approve that as the pinned model for pilot, pending Sofia's benchmark and our prompt-set pass rates.
[08:40] Sofia Martinez: Great. I'll run three runs: FP16 baseline, 4-bit quant candidate, and non-quant. I'll capture p50/p95 latency, token-cost, and a quality score against your prompt set.
[08:58] Mark Davis: For the quality score — can you surface exact-match, BLEU-ish and a simple hallucination metric we can use?
[09:10] Sofia Martinez: We'll compute exact-match on structured outputs, and a simple false-positives hallucination count for free-text. Not a perfect metric but good for gating.
[09:25] Olivia Chen: On rollout automation — how fast can we switch traffic if the model starts regressing? We need <10 minutes for a rollback window ideally.
[09:36] Alex Chen: Automated rollback via policy can be near-instant; switching the pinned model in Console is immediate for new traffic. For existing in-flight requests, you'll let them finish. We'll document expected propagation times.
[09:52] Priya Rao: Does Redwood support traffic splitting for canaries?
[09:58] Sofia Martinez: Yes, you can define a traffic split and percentage ramp schedules. Also metric-based automatic ramp or halt.
[10:10] Mark Davis: Security question — how are model artifacts stored and who can access the model binaries? We are sensitive about export controls.
[10:20] Alex Chen: For hosted, model artifacts are stored in Redwood's secure artifact storage. Access is RBAC-controlled; we can restrict who in your org and within Redwood has access. For private deployment customers you keep artifacts on your infrastructure. We also integrate with KMS for keys and provide audit trails.
[10:40] Priya Rao: We'll need SOC2 type detail and where the keys are stored.
[10:44] Alex Chen: I'll send the SOC2 and KMS integration docs after the call.
[10:52] [11:00] Olivia Chen: Back to metrics — what does the console present for fallbacks? Can we see rollback events and which requests hit each model id?
[11:07] Sofia Martinez: Yes, Console has per-request metadata, token-level cost, and route decision. We keep a time-series of fallback events and can export raw logs.
[11:20] Mark Davis: Great. For the benchmarking run, can you use our SSH-accessible load generator or do you want us to upload samples?
[11:28] Sofia Martinez: Upload the sample traffic shape and a small corpus of prompts; we'll run from our test infra to match region and concurrency. If you want to run from your side as well we can share the benchmark config so you can reproduce.
[11:40] Priya Rao: We'll upload by Friday.
[11:44] Alex Chen: Perfect. Any regulator-specific needs? Data residency?
[11:49] Priya Rao: Not yet, but logs for audit must remain in the EU for a subset of test users. We'll mark that in the requirement doc.
[12:00] Sofia Martinez: We can scope a private-region pilot or config routing by region.
[12:07] Olivia Chen: Okay next steps recap?
[12:10] Alex Chen: Recap: Sofia runs benchmarks and shares sheet (due 6/02). Priya/Mark upload prompt set and traffic sample (due 5/29). Alex sends security/KMS docs (due 5/28). We'll schedule a canary rollout review for 6/09.
[12:30] Priya Rao: That matches. One last question — if we pin to FP16 and later decide to move to 4-bit, what validation do you recommend?
[12:40] Sofia Martinez: Run A/B on a shadow set first, validate exact-match thresholds, run user-facing QA, then incrementally ramp. Keep the non-quantized model as a safety net during ramp.
[12:55] Alex Chen: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the benchmark sheet and links.
[13:00] Priya Rao: Thanks, talk soon.
---
Notes: Links to be shared after call: security/KMS doc, sample policy templates for routing, benchmark spreadsheet.
